newsitem.title: USA: NYS lawmakers plan more fundraisers - report.
newsitem.headline: NYS lawmakers plan more fundraisers - report.

text.p: New York State lawmakers looked on their way to holding a record series of fundraising events in 1997, the year the state's lobbying rules expire, though they may get less money, a nonprofit group said Monday.

A total of 180 fundraising events were planned in the legislative year, eight more than the previous year, but "minimum contributions" only added up to $45,699, falling short of the $57,890 mark set in 1996.

The final sum could be higher or lower, as the term minimum contributions refers to how much lawmakers suggest lobbyists give on invitations, according to the New York Public Interest Group (NYPIRG), which prepared the report.

The group, which calls itself a nonpartisan watchdog for good government, had Gov George Pataki down for three events, with minimum contibutions ranging from $19.97 to $1,000, Senate Majority Leader, Joseph Bruno, R-Troy holding two, and Assembly Speaker Sheldon Silver, D-Manhattan, planning four events, two of which were with Democratic Assembly Campaign Committees.
Blair Horner, legislative director for NYPIRG, said no conclusions could be drawn from the data about whether Democrats or Republicans were more likely to hold fundraisers.

"It's everybody, this is just part of the New York State Incumbency Protection Act. The one thing you don't see is any challengers." Aside from the leaders, the study focused on events held in Albany, as those seemed directed at lobbyists, unlike fundraisers held by lawmakers in their own districts for constituents, which were not seen as posing the same sorts of conflicts of interest questions, he added.
Spokesmen for the Republican governor, Senate Majority Leader, and the Assembly Speaker, were not immediately available to comment.

Saying its data showed New York State had one of the most toothless laws in the nation, as it focuses on disclosure, the group has thrown its support behind a proposed new bill, the Integrity in Government Act. It added Common Cause/New York, the League of Women Voters in New York, and United We Stand America state chapter also back the measure.

That legislation would ban lobbyists from making campaign contributions when the legislature is in session and meeting regularly, Horner said. Lobbyists also would face stiffer disclosure rules. Elected lawmakers would be banned from accepting gifts and honoria, and the state's 20-year old Temporary Commission on Lobbying would be made permanent, added the legislative director of NYPIRG.
"We have a tactical advantage because the law expires this year, so lawmakers have to vote," he added.
